body_markdown:
An MCP server is a connector that lets an AI assistant like Claude or ChatGPT use one of your apps. The best ones for non-developers are official and hosted. If a server asks you to install code or run a command, skip it. If you click "Connect" and log in to the app's own company, it belongs on your list.


## The short version


Pick servers you add by logging in, not by installing anything.


Only add servers published by the company that owns the app.


A server can do anything the permissions you grant allow, so read the login screen.


On Floot, one server builds and hosts a whole app from a description.


Elsewhere, building an app means stitching a database, logins, and a host together.


The rest of this guide covers what an MCP server is, the best picks by job, which to add first, and how to add one.


## An MCP server, in one picture


Think of an adapter plug. Your AI assistant is the laptop, and your apps are outlets it does not fit.


An MCP server is the adapter for one app. Plug in the Notion adapter, and your AI can edit your Notion pages. Plug in Stripe's, and it can look up your payments. (MCP, short for Model Context Protocol, is the plug shape every adapter shares.)


The split exists so each app company controls its own adapter, and you choose which to plug in. More in.


## The best MCP servers, by job


Every pick needs no terminal and is in Claude's directory (more than 375 connectors as of July 2026) or hosted by its vendor.


## Google Drive and Notion


They search and summarize your documents, and Notion's also edits pages. Notion runs its own hosted server. Try: "Turn last month's pricing notes into a one-page summary."


## Gmail and Google Calendar


They search threads, draft replies, and find or create meetings. Both appear in Claude's connector settings. Try: "Draft replies to this week's unanswered investor emails, but do not send them."


## Slack, Linear, and Asana


They read channels and tasks and create issues. Linear publishes an official hosted endpoint, and all three are in Claude's directory.


## Canva and Figma


Canva's server, hosted at mcp.canva.com, creates and edits designs. Figma's reads design files, and its remote server has been in beta with limited access.


## Stripe


It looks up customers, payments, and subscriptions, and creates payment links. Stripe hosts it at mcp.stripe.com. Try: "How many subscriptions canceled this month?"


## Context7


It feeds current software documentation to the AI, free, from mcp.context7.com. It is mainly for developers.


## Floot


It turns your AI into an app builder that hosts what it builds. Floot is ours, and it is covered below.


Notice the pattern. Every pick except Floot works on something you already have: a doc, an inbox, a payment.


## Which should you add first?


Here is the quick test. Ask which app you open first every morning.


If you work mostly in one place, like email or docs, you can skip the rest for now.


If you keep copying information between apps, you need the server for each one. That covers call notes going into Linear, announcements becoming Canva posts, and "how are sales?" answered from Stripe.


If the tool you need does not exist yet, you need a builder, not another connector.


## What each tool makes you do


Adding a server is a few clicks in both assistants.


In Claude, open Customize, then Connectors, pick a server, and log in to the app. An unlisted server goes in as a custom connector URL, and the Free plan allows one.


In ChatGPT, connectors live in the Plugins directory (merged with the app directory on July 9, 2026). Unlisted servers need developer mode, in beta on Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu, with full write access only on Business, Enterprise, and Edu.


The pattern is the same everywhere it goes wrong: the official server does not do what you want, so you paste in a lookalike URL from a forum, and it logs in as you.


Floot is the MCP server for building apps, and it is the only kind on this list that leaves something running. Every other server here lets your AI read or change something that already exists: a doc, a calendar, a payment. Floot lets it create a new app: pages, small server programs called endpoints ("add a signup," "email the weekly report"), and a Postgres database, hosted on a live URL from the first build.


Because Floot also includes the database, logins with Google, Microsoft, and email, file storage, email sending, scheduled jobs, and live updates, you add one server instead of stitching a database, a login service, and a host together. You never sign up for anything else, and building through Claude or ChatGPT adds no second AI bill. More in.


## FAQ


## What are the best MCP servers for beginners?


Google Drive, Gmail, Google Calendar, and Notion. They need no terminal and help with work you already do every day.


## Can I use MCP servers without coding?


Yes. You add remote servers in Claude's or ChatGPT's settings by logging in.


## Which MCP server should I install first?


The one tied to the app you open most, usually email or docs.


## Are MCP servers free?


Most official connectors cost nothing extra, though some features need the app's paid plan.


## Are MCP servers safe?


Official ones are as safe as the permissions you grant. The bigger risk is prompt injection, so keep approvals on.


## Does Floot work as an MCP server?


Yes. With Floot connected, you describe an app in Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor, and Floot builds and hosts it.
